content: Chronic cold urticaria, commonly referred to as cold hives, is a condition characterized by the development of hives or large, red, raised welts on the skin. These welts are often itchy, and in many cases, the hands and feet may also become swollen and itchy. The size of the hives can range from as small as a pencil eraser to as large as a quarter or even larger. When the condition persists for more than six weeks, it is classified as chronic. The course of the disease is unpredictable, and while it can last a lifetime, it most commonly affects individuals between the ages of 18 and 25. The primary symptoms of cold urticaria include red welts, wheals, or hives that can appear on the skin or mucous membranes. These hives may or may not be itchy and can last anywhere from a few minutes to several days, varying significantly between individuals. A burning sensation is also commonly reported. In severe cases, the condition can lead to hypotension, which is potentially life-threatening. Severe reactions are more likely to occur if hives develop within three minutes of exposure to cold stimuli, as observed during a cold test. The underlying cause of cold urticaria is a histamine-mediated reaction triggered by exposure to cold stimuli, such as a sudden drop in temperature, cold air, or cold water. While the majority of cases are idiopathic, meaning no specific cause can be identified, some rare conditions may contribute to the development of cold hives. In such cases, further testing may be warranted to rule out these underlying conditions. Diagnosis is typically made by an allergist or other licensed healthcare professional through a cold test. This involves placing a piece of ice against the forearm for three to five minutes. A positive result is indicated by the appearance of raised, red hives at the site of contact. These hives may take the shape of the ice or radiate outward from the area of contact. The most critical aspect of managing cold urticaria is avoiding exposure to cold environments and staying warm. Air-conditioned rooms and cold pools may exacerbate symptoms, and immediate warming of the skin can help alleviate itching. Antihistamines such as diphenhydramine (Benadryl), cetirizine (Zyrtec), or fexofenadine (Allegra) can be used to prevent or treat hives. However, cold urticaria can lead to severe systemic reactions, including anaphylaxis, which may be life-threatening. For this reason, individuals with cold urticaria are often advised to carry an injectable form of epinephrine, such as an EpiPen or Twinject, for emergency use. It is important to note that reactions can occur even on warm days if sweat on the skin is rapidly cooled by a breeze, leading to the development of hives. In such cases, quickly drying the skin and covering up can help control the reaction before it worsens. Swimming poses a particular danger, as the combination of a rapid heart rate and the onset of hives can result in hypotension. Taking an antihistamine before entering cold water and conserving energy until the body adjusts to the temperature may help reduce the risk of a severe reaction. Contrary to popular belief, immersing the affected area in hot water or moving to a warmer environment does not improve the condition.
